title: Why does a private field with a getter that returns the live internal collection (e.g. getPermissions() returning the backing List) NOT give real encapsulation (caller can mutate via getPermissions().add()), and how do you fix it (unmodifiableList or defensive copy)?
shortTitle: Why does returning a live collection break encapsulation?

s1_definition.profdef: Making a field `private` is NOT enough for encapsulation if the getter returns a REFERENCE to the live internal collection. The caller receives the SAME list object that the class uses internally. `account.getTransactions().add(fakeTransaction)` — the caller just added a fake transaction to the REAL internal list, bypassing ALL validation. The field is private, but the REFERENCE to the mutable object leaked. Two fixes: (1) `Collections.unmodifiableList(transactions)` — returns a read-only VIEW; `add()` throws UnsupportedOperationException. (2) `new ArrayList<>(transactions)` — returns a DEFENSIVE COPY; caller modifies the copy, internal list is unaffected. `List.copyOf(transactions)` (Java 10) does both: creates an unmodifiable copy.
s1_definition.analogy: The vault (private field) is locked. But the bank gives Rajesh a KEY to the vault (reference via getter). Rajesh walks in and adds fake gold bars (fakeTransaction) — the vault is "private" but its contents are MODIFIED through the leaked key! Fix 1: give Rajesh a PHOTO of the vault contents (unmodifiable view — he can look but not touch). Fix 2: give Rajesh a COPY of the contents (defensive copy — he can do whatever with the copy; the vault is unaffected).
s1_definition.oneliner: private + getter returning live collection = FAKE encapsulation. Caller mutates internals via reference. Fix: return unmodifiableList (read-only view) or defensive copy (new ArrayList<>(list)). List.copyOf() = unmodifiable + copy.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Making a field `private` is NOT enough for encapsulation if the getter returns a REFERENCE to the live internal collection. The caller receives the SAME list object that the class uses internally. `account.getTransactions().add(fakeTransaction)` — the caller just added a fake transaction to the REAL internal list, bypassing ALL validation. The field is private, but the REFERENCE to the mutable object leaked. Two fixes: (1) `Collections.unmodifiableList(transactions)` — returns a read-only VIEW; `add()` throws UnsupportedOperationException. (2) `new ArrayList<>(transactions)` — returns a DEFENSIVE COPY; caller modifies the copy, internal list is unaffected. `List.copyOf(transactions)` (Java 10) does both: creates an unmodifiable copy.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The vault (private field) is locked. But the bank gives Rajesh a KEY to the vault (reference via getter). Rajesh walks in and adds fake gold bars (fakeTransaction) — the vault is "private" but its contents are MODIFIED through the leaked key! Fix 1: give Rajesh a PHOTO of the vault contents (unmodifiable view — he can look but not touch). Fix 2: give Rajesh a COPY of the contents (defensive copy — he can do whatever with the copy; the vault is unaffected).

**One line to remember:** private + getter returning live collection = FAKE encapsulation. Caller mutates internals via reference. Fix: return unmodifiableList (read-only view) or defensive copy (new ArrayList<>(list)). List.copyOf() = unmodifiable + copy.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The bank's Account class has a "private" transactions list with a getter that returns the live reference.** A reporting module called `account.getTransactions()` and accidentally called `.clear()` on the returned list — wiping all transaction history for 500 accounts in production. Another module called `.add(fakeTransaction)` to test a display format — the fake transaction persisted in the real account. Both bypassed the `addTransaction()` method that validates, audits, and notifies. Fix: return `List.copyOf(transactions)` — unmodifiable copy. Fake adds and accidental clears are IMPOSSIBLE.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1 — Broken.** BrokenAccount.getTransactions() returns the LIVE internal ArrayList reference. Caller calls `.add(fakeTransaction)` — fake transaction added to the REAL list. No validation. No audit. "Private" field modified from outside.

**Step 2 — Broken worse.** Caller calls `.clear()` — ALL transactions wiped. 500 accounts lost their entire history. No authorization check. No recovery.

**Step 3 — Fix: unmodifiable view.** `Collections.unmodifiableList(transactions)` wraps the list in a read-only proxy. `.add()` → UnsupportedOperationException. `.clear()` → UnsupportedOperationException. Internal list protected.

**Step 4 — Fix: defensive copy.** `new ArrayList<>(transactions)` returns a separate list. Caller's `.add()` and `.clear()` affect ONLY the copy. Internal list unaffected.

**Step 5 — Fix: immutable elements.** Transaction is a record (immutable). Even if caller gets a reference to a Transaction object, they CANNOT modify its amount or type. Unmodifiable list + immutable elements = TRUE encapsulation.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ BROKEN: leaky getter ═══

  Account { private List<Transaction> transactions; }
    │
    getTransactions() → returns SAME reference (0x1234)
    │
    caller.getTransactions().add(fake)  → modifies list at 0x1234!
    caller.getTransactions().clear()    → wipes list at 0x1234!
    ← ENCAPSULATION BROKEN!

  ═══ FIXED: defensive return ═══

  SafeAccount { private List<Transaction> transactions; }
    │
    FIX 1: unmodifiableList(transactions) → read-only wrapper
           .add() → UnsupportedOperationException!

    FIX 2: new ArrayList<>(transactions) → separate copy
           .add() → affects copy only. Internal safe.

    FIX 3: List.copyOf(transactions)     → unmodifiable + copy
           .add() → UnsupportedOperationException + internal safe.

    FIX 4: transactions.stream()         → read-only pipeline
           Can filter/map/collect. Cannot modify source.

  ═══ COMPLETE PROTECTION ═══
  Unmodifiable list   → blocks add/remove/clear
  Immutable elements  → blocks element mutation (record = no setters)
  Both together       → TRUE encapsulation (Recommended) 
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A private field with a getter that returns the live internal collection is FAKE encapsulation. The caller receives a reference to the same mutable object — `getTransactions().add(fake)` bypasses all validation, and `getTransactions().clear()` wipes the internal state. The field is private but its CONTENTS are fully accessible and modifiable through the leaked reference.

In my banking demo, BrokenAccount's getter returns the live ArrayList. A reporting module accidentally called `.clear()` — wiping transaction history for 500 accounts. SafeAccount fixes this three ways: `Collections.unmodifiableList()` returns a read-only view (add/clear throw UnsupportedOperationException), `new ArrayList<>(transactions)` returns a defensive copy (caller modifies the copy only), and `List.copyOf()` combines both (unmodifiable AND a separate copy). Transaction is a record (immutable) — even if the caller gets a Transaction reference, they cannot modify its amount.

The complete protection recipe: (1) private field — controls who declares the reference, (2) no direct setter for the collection — only validated methods like addTransaction(), (3) getter returns unmodifiable or copy — prevents structural mutations through the reference, (4) immutable elements (records, final fields) — prevents element-level mutations. All four together = TRUE encapsulation. In production Spring services, always return `List.copyOf()` or `Collections.unmodifiableList()` from getters that expose internal collections.
